papers.title: Function-on-Function Bayesian Optimization
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has been widely used to optimize expensive and gradient-free objective functions across various domains. However, existing BO methods have not addressed the objective where both inputs and outputs are functions, which increasingly arise in complex systems as advanced sensing technologies. To fill this gap, we propose a novel function-on-function Bayesian optimization (FFBO) framework. Specifically, we first introduce a function-on-function Gaussian process (FFGP) model with a separable operator-valued kernel to capture the correlations between function-valued inputs and outputs. Compared to existing Gaussian process models, FFGP is modeled directly in the function space. Based on FFGP, we define a scalar upper confidence bound (UCB) acquisition function using a weighted operator-based scalarization strategy. Then, a scalable functional gradient ascent algorithm (FGA) is developed to efficiently identify the optimal function-valued input. We further analyze the theoretical properties of the proposed method. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the superior performance of FFBO over existing approaches.

papers.title: DIVIDE: A Framework for Learning from Independent Multi-Mechanism Data Using Deep Encoders and Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: Scientific datasets often arise from multiple independent mechanisms such as spatial, categorical or structural effects, whose combined influence obscures their individual contributions. We introduce DIVIDE, a framework that disentangles these influences by integrating mechanism-specific deep encoders with a structured Gaussian Process in a joint latent space. Disentanglement here refers to separating independently acting generative factors. The encoders isolate distinct mechanisms while the Gaussian Process captures their combined effect with calibrated uncertainty. The architecture supports structured priors, enabling interpretable and mechanism-aware prediction as well as efficient active learning. DIVIDE is demonstrated on synthetic datasets combining categorical image patches with nonlinear spatial fields, on FerroSIM spin lattice simulations of ferroelectric patterns, and on experimental PFM hysteresis loops from PbTiO3 films. Across benchmarks, DIVIDE separates mechanisms, reproduces additive and scaled interactions, and remains robust under noise. The framework extends naturally to multifunctional datasets where mechanical, electromagnetic or optical responses coexist.

papers.title: SetupKit: Efficient Multi-Corner Setup/Hold Time Characterization Using Bias-Enhanced Interpolation and Active Learning
papers.abstract: Accurate setup/hold time characterization is crucial for modern chip timing closure, but its reliance on potentially millions of SPICE simulations across diverse process-voltagetemperature (PVT) corners creates a major bottleneck, often lasting weeks or months. Existing methods suffer from slow search convergence and inefficient exploration, especially in the multi-corner setting. We introduce SetupKit, a novel framework designed to break this bottleneck using statistical intelligence, circuit analysis and active learning (AL). SetupKit integrates three key innovations: BEIRA, a bias-enhanced interpolation search derived from statistical error modeling to accelerate convergence by overcoming stagnation issues, initial search interval estimation by circuit analysis and AL strategy using Gaussian Process. This AL component intelligently learns PVT-timing correlations, actively guiding the expensive simulations to the most informative corners, thus minimizing redundancy in multicorner characterization. Evaluated on industrial 22nm standard cells across 16 PVT corners, SetupKit demonstrates a significant 2.4x overall CPU time reduction (from 720 to 290 days on a single core) compared to standard practices, drastically cutting characterization time. SetupKit offers a principled, learningbased approach to library characterization, addressing a critical EDA challenge and paving the way for more intelligent simulation management.

papers.title: An Active Learning Interatomic Potential For Defect-Engineered CoCrFeMnNi High-Entropy Alloy
papers.abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit exceptional properties arising from a combination of thermodynamic, kinetic and structural factors and have found applications in numerous fields such as aerospace, energy, chemical industries, hydrogen storage, and ocean engineering. However, a large compositional space remains to be explored. Unlike conventional approaches, computational methods have shown accelerated discovery of novel alloys in a short time. However, the lack of interatomic potentials have posed a challenge in discovering new alloy compositions and property measurements. In the present work, we have developed a Moment Tensor Potential (MTP) trained by Machine Learning based approach using the BFGS unconstrained optimization algorithm for the CoCrFeMnNi High-entropy alloy. Our training set consists of various defects induced configurations such as vacancies, dislocations and stacking-faults. An active learning scheme to re-train the potential was undertaken to dynamically to add training data upon encountering extrapolative configurations during non-equilibrium simulations. A thorough investigation of the error metrics, equation of state, uniaxial tensile deformation, nano-indentation and solid-liquid interface stability for this alloy was carried out, and it is seen that the MTP potential outperforms the popular Modified Embedded Atom Method (MEAM) potential on physical properties prediction. The accuracy and high computational speed are discussed using scaling performance. The potential is prepared for public use by embedding it into the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) code.

papers.title: xLSTM-PINN: Memory-Gated Spectral Remodeling for Physics-Informed Learning
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINN) face significant challenges from spectral bias, which impedes their ability to model high-frequency phenomena and limits extrapolation performance. To address this, we introduce xLSTM-PINN, a novel architecture that performs representation-level spectral remodeling through memory gating and residual micro-steps. Our method consistently achieves markedly lower spectral error and root mean square error (RMSE) across four diverse partial differential equation (PDE) benchmarks, along withhhh a broader stable learning-rate window. Frequency-domain analysis confirms that xLSTM-PINN elevates high-frequency kernel weights, shifts the resolvable bandwidth rightward, and shortens the convergence time for high-wavenumber components. Without modifying automatic differentiation or physics loss constraints, this work provides a robust pathway to suppress spectral bias, thereby improving accuracy, reproducibility, and transferability in physics-informed learning.

papers.title: Compression Behavior of M2052 Alloy Lattice Structures Fabricated by Selective Laser Melting
papers.abstract: The M2052 alloy (Mn‐20Cu‐5Ni‐2Fe at%) exhibits excellent damping capacity and favorable mechanical strength, making it a promising candidate for vibration damping and energy absorption. However, its potential in lattice structures has not been reported to date. In this article, M2052 alloy lattice structures are fabricated via selective laser melting to evaluate their mechanical properties and energy absorption capabilities. Three lattice architectures with comparable relative densities are designed and manufactured: body‐centered cubic (BCC), BCC with vertical struts (BCCZ), and reinforced hollow BCCZ (RHBCCZ) featuring hollow struts and strengthening ribs. Quasi‐static compression tests and finite element simulations are conducted to analyze their mechanical responses and deformation mechanisms. Furthermore, the effects of heat treatment on the compressive properties and microstructural evolution of BCC lattices are investigated. Results demonstrate that the RHBCCZ structure delivers optimal performance, with a Young's modulus of 1506.3 MPa, yield strength of 18.41 MPa, and maximum energy absorption of 22.69 J cm −3 . Heat treatment enhanced the yield strength and altered the deformation mode of the lattice. This article highlights the potential of M2052 alloy in load‐bearing, energy‐absorbing, and lightweight structural applications.

papers.title: Lungprint: Robot-Assisted 3D Bioprinting of Lung Models With Cellulose-Derivative Bioinks
papers.abstract: Abstract Respiratory diseases remain a leading cause of mortality worldwide, underscoring the need for better models to study lung function and therapy. Yet the lung’s intricate branched structure and dynamic motion make it difficult to recreate realistic in vitro lung models. Recent advances in 3D bioprinting offer unprecedented control in fabricating complex, tissue-like structures, holding promise for replicating airway geometry and mechanics. This work leverages a six-axis robotic bioprinting system to construct biomimetic lung airways using novel hybrid hydrogels infused with nanomaterials. Traditional three-axis printers build layers on a fixed plane, which can lead to irregularities in overhanging structures. In contrast, a robotic six-degree-of-freedom printer can deposit bioink from multiple orientations, enabling seamless fabrication of curved, hollow airway segments that better emulate native lung architecture. We formulate and evaluate several hydrogel-based bioinks blending alginate and carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC)—a cellulose derivative, to optimize print fidelity and mechanical integrity. The robotic printer’s multi-directional capability ensures uniform wall thickness and smooth curvature in printed airways. Print parameters are systematically tuned to improve geometric accuracy and structural support in these soft constructs. The resulting 3D-printed printed airway branch, a small segment of a full lung model, exhibits enhanced flexibility and biocompatibility, approximating the softness and resilience of real lung tissue. By integrating advanced biofabrication materials with robotic precision, this study establishes a new paradigm for in vitro lung modeling. These biofabricated lung analogues enable more realistic studies of particle deposition, inhalation toxicology, and targeted drug delivery, effectively bridging engineering innovation with pulmonary medicine

papers.title: Coupled DEM-CFD Numerical Simulations of IN718 Deposition on a Ti6Al4V Substrate via Laser Powder Bed Fusion
papers.abstract: Abstract The integration of dissimilar materials presents significant challenges due to the inherent differences in thermal and mechanical properties between the two materials. The joining of IN718 and Ti6Al4V is particularly challenging due to the formation of brittle Ni-Ti intermetallic phases, Ti2Ni, TiNi, and Ni3Ti, and elemental segregation during the fusion of the two materials. The presence of brittle phases significantly decreases the bonding strength of the multi-material components, resulting in severe cracking and delamination between the two materials. This study investigates the deposition of IN718 single tracks on Ti6Al4V substrates using a thermofluidic simulation framework that couples the discrete element method (DEM) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD). A parametric study is conducted to analyze the effects of laser power (200-370W), scanning speed (810-1100 mm/s), and laser frequency (continuous/pulsing) on melt pool dimensions and defect formation during Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF). These variables provide a means of controlling the energy density reaching the powder bed, consequently influencing the melting mode (conduction, transition, or keyhole), and ultimately dictating the melt pool dynamics and extent of mixing between the two materials. The model successfully captures key physical phenomena, including melt consolidation, Marangoni convection, surface tension gradients, recoil pressure, and evaporation-driven instabilities. A particular focus is placed on understanding how these forces contribute to defect formation, such as keyhole formation, and lack of fusion defects. The variation in the extent of mixing between the two immiscible materials at various processing parameters is also investigated.

papers.title: The Effects of Process Parameters on Nanoparticle Distribution and Microstructure Formation During Selective Laser Melting
papers.abstract: Abstract Selective laser melting (SLM) offers unique opportunities to produce aluminum-matrix nanocomposites by dispersing ceramic nanoparticles within AlSi10Mg powder and fusing successive layers with a high-power laser. In this work, a coupled 3D computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and 2D cellular automata (CA) model is applied to quantify how key process parameters—laser power, scan speed, and preheating temperature influence molten-pool behavior, nanoparticle dispersion, and resulting microstructure. The CFD simulation captures transient heat transfer, Marangoni- and buoyancy-driven convection, and distribution of TiB2 nanoparticles in an AlSi10Mg matrix. Temperature and flow fields computed in transverse planes are mapped into the 2D CA microstructure model to simulate grain evolution with and without nanoparticle-induced heterogeneous nucleation. Results show that decreasing scan speed or increasing laser power enlarges the molten pool, heightens peak surface temperature, and intensifies Marangoni convection, which in turn drives strong recirculation vortices that centrifugally eject nanoparticles from vortex cores, creating localized particle-void zones. By contrast, higher preheating temperature modestly enlarges the pool but yields a minor variation in molten pool convection. When nanoparticles serve as nucleation sites, regions of uniform particle dispersion solidify into fine equiaxed grains, while voided pockets yield coarser columnar or equiaxed structures. Across all parameter variations, the introduction of nanoparticles reduces average grain diameter by 30%–40% relative to nanoparticle-free simulations.

papers.title: Acoustic Cell Patterning-Assisted Digital Light Processing for Bioprinting Anisotropic Tissues
papers.abstract: Abstract Bioprinting technology has developed to be a powerful tool for regenerative medicine, tissue engineering, and drug screening. Unlike conventional scaffold fabrication techniques, bioprinting allows for the generation of intricate geometries that closely resemble native tissue architecture. Current various bioprinting techniques include inkjet bioprinting, extrusion-based bioprinting, laser-assisted bioprinting, droplet-based bioprinting, and stereolithography-based bioprinting. However, achieving biomimetic anisotropic characteristics of living tissues remains a significant challenge. To achieve precise control cell alignment and orientation during the bioprinting process, we introduce an acoustic patterning method that can integrate with laser-assisted bioprinting to generate anisotropic-engineered tissues. Here, the bioink consists of the GelMA solution blended with living cells. Our acoustic patterning device comprises pairs of piezoelectric transducers and a Petri dish. Standing acoustic waves generated by transducers manipulate and align cells within the bioink during the time interval of the bioprinting process. Through proof-of-concept experiments, we validated the patterning effects of our acoustic patterning device and the printing ability of our bioprinting platform in terms of printing resolution, three-dimensional (3D) scalability, and anisotropic printing capabilities. The results show this platform successfully produced 3D constructs ranging from millimeter to centimeter scale, including structures such as cones, nerve conduits, and vascular branches. Additionally, we assessed the viability and morphology of NIH 3T3 fibroblast cells within the printed constructs. The results indicated high cell viability and proper cellular extension in the engineered tissues. In conclusion, we anticipate this platform to offer new possibilities for 3D bioprinting applications in regenerative medicine, tissue engineering, and biomedical research.

papers.title: Permeability Evaluation of Laser Powder Bed Fusion Printed Wick Structures for Passive Heat Transfer in Space Applications
papers.abstract: Abstract High-performance wick structures are essential for advancing passive two-phase heat transfer devices, especially for space applications. In this study, cylindrical lattice wick structures, measuring 20mm in diameter and 40mm in height, were fabricated from Inconel 718 using Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS). Inconel was chosen because of its exceptional durability, high temperature strength, and resistance to corrosion and oxidation. These properties ensure the rapidly changing environment in space will have little to no effect on the material. DMLS, an advanced additive manufacturing technique, allows for precise control over the geometric features and fabrication. Additionally, using DMLS for wick structures gives the opportunity for rapid reproduction and design improvements. These structures were designed using nTopology, which is an implicit modeling software with field driven design that gives intricate control over the design process to produce advanced geometries. These samples included two different distinct geometries: body centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC). Lattice structures provide the ability to tailor the porosity, which enables a more uniform control for fluid movement. Lattice also has greater mechanical strength and is easily customizable, which makes small adjustments seamless. This study was primarily focused on the permeability of the additively manufactured wick structures, which is a crucial property affecting their capillary fluid transport capability. Permeability, which measures the ease of fluid flow through a porous structure, was evaluated using experimental methods and compared against theoretical predictions. A laminar flow loop was designed that incorporated a water reservoir, pump, flowmeter, and a custom 3D-designed and resin-printed sample holder to secure the sample. Pressure sensors were aligned on both sides of the sample holder to measure the differential pressure. This allowed permeability calculations based on Darcy’s Law. A Taguchi experiment design was used to optimize testing conditions, which focused on three different variables: flow rate, porosity of the sample, and differential pressure. The results from this study demonstrate that permeability can be adjusted by optimizing the parameters of additive manufacturing and the geometry of the lattices. These findings highlight the potential for wick structures to enhance the performance of a thermal management system in space applications. In addition to space applications, this research benefits cooling-technologies used in heat pipes for high performance electronics. Future work will focus on refining and validating different permeability models under varying conditions, including microgravity. Understanding the behavior in reduced gravity will help refine the parameters when relevant to space applications.

papers.title: Tuning the Young’s modulus of gelatin methacryloyl hydrogels with masked stereolithography bioprinting
papers.abstract: The mechanical properties of the extracellular matrix (ECM) are critical regulators of cell behavior. Native tissues span a broad mechanical spectrum, ranging from soft brain tissue to stiff bone and often exhibit a spatial heterogeneity in stiffness. To replicate these complex microenvironments in vitro , biomaterials must offer not only tunable stiffness but also spatial control over mechanical properties within three-dimensional (3D) constructs. Gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) hydrogels are widely used in biofabrication. Due to their photopolymerizability, their stiffness can be modulated by altering the material composition and exposure to light. However, so far no bioprinting platform has integrated these tuning parameters to fabricate complex 3D constructs with spatially controlled mechanical properties. In this study, we demonstrate the use of a masked stereolithography bioprinter (mSLAb) to systematically tune the Young's modulus (YM) of 3D printed GelMA hydrogel constructs. Systematic variations in YM are achieved by adjusting the material composition. Furthermore, the mSLAb allows for tuning of the YM during the printing process by varying the light exposure and intensity, enabling the creation of YM gradients within the 3D construct. The mSLAb thus allows for generating a predefined 3D structure which mechanical properties can be modified during the printing process. With this approach, we achieved a stiffness range, spanning from roughly 1 kPa to over 200 kPa. These results establish mSLAb as a powerful platform for engineering mechanically customizable and structurally complex hydrogel constructs, with cell-instructive YM gradients with high spatial precision. • Young's modulus (YM) of GelMA is tuned using a masked stereolithography bioprinter (mSLAb). • Material composition and energy density are factors for tuning the YM using mSLAb. • mSLAb enables printing of complex 3D structures with spatially tuned stiffness.

papers.title: Numerical Investigation of Multi-Track Laser in Metal Additive Manufacturing for Inconel 718 Defect-Free Components
papers.abstract: Abstract Metal additive manufacturing (MAM), particularly laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), has become indispensable for producing complex geometries in high-performance materials like nickel-based superalloys. While offering design freedom and reduced lead times, LPBF parts often contain defects (porosity, residual stresses) that impair mechanical properties. This challenge is especially critical for Inconel 718 (IN718), a widely used aerospace alloy valued for its strength and thermal resistance but difficult to process conventionally. We utilize Flow-3D’s Additive Manufacturing (AM) module to simulate single- and multi-track LPBF processes across key energy densities. Results show: (1) melt pool depth correlates strongly with energy density while width exhibits complex behavior, (2) our model outperforms eight NIST Benchmark models in melt pool prediction accuracy, and (3) optimal parameters for stable melt pools are identified. The developed high-fidelity simulation framework advances beyond single-track studies by enabling multi-layer analysis of real printing conditions. This provides manufacturers with a practical tool to minimize defects in IN718 components, bridging a critical gap between research and industrial application.

papers.title: Enabling On-Demand Aerospace Component Manufacturing: Topology Optimization of GE Engine Bracket and Fabrication Using Metal FFF
papers.abstract: Abstract Additive Manufacturing (AM) offers advantages over conventional manufacturing processes, particularly by reducing the number of parts produced through multistage combined technologies, but these often result in low manufacturing yields or require post-processing. AM facilitates the production of complex geometries with fine features, overhangs, and lattice structures. For instance, Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) technology enables the fabrication of intricate parts that can be easily post-processed by removing residual powder. Laser powder bed AM technologies are widely discussed in the literature due to their design freedom in creating complex geometries, with and without the need for support generation. However, rapid solidification due to a thermal gradient in the build direction, which leads to the formation of columnar grains and warpage, is one of the challenges. To address this challenge, we propose layer-by-layer metal FFF technology, followed by the debinding and sintering process, as an alternative to powder- and laser-based approaches. Furthermore, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM) principles are discussed to minimize the need for support generation and enable easy post-processing, thereby improving surface finish to meet high tolerances in fabricating components for aerospace and healthcare applications. In this paper, we discuss strategies for aerospace component manufacturing to address the challenges of fabricating parts with intricate features and complex geometries. This primarily includes applying topology optimization to reduce the weight of the GE jet engine bracket without compromising structural rigidity and functionality, along with support assessment, fill density, material selection, and process optimization to improve overall manufacturability. The topology optimization was performed in SOLIDWORKS 2024 R2 in a high-fidelity environment, and the fabricated parts were validated under the specified loading conditions. Weight reductions of 44%, 50%, and 60% were achieved relative to the original part. Simulations and design validation were performed to verify structural rigidity, strength, and the integrity of the clamping features under the applied loading conditions. The topology optimized parts were manufactured on Markforged’s Metal X 3D printing system and evaluated for precision in achieving fillet radii (compared with CAD models), hole and cavity accuracy, dimensional accuracy, and process efficiency. To conclude, topology optimization was successfully applied to the GE engine bracket and validated under the applied loading conditions, achieving a 60% weight reduction from the original design while maintaining the part’s performance and strength. Dimensional accuracy analysis further demonstrated the manufacturability and capabilities of metal FFF technology for aerospace applications.

papers.title: Investigation of Skewed Sinusoidal Cavities in Additively Manufactured Rotors of Electric Machines
papers.abstract: This study investigates the use of additive manufacturing (AM), particularly selective laser melting (SLM), to enhance the performance of permanent-magnet synchronous machines (PMSMs) through innovative rotor designs featuring skewed sinusoidal cavities. By enabling complex geometries, AM reduces torque pulsations and acoustic noise emission and eddy current losses, improving efficiency and torque quality in PMSMs. Using the finite element method (FEM), we evaluate various skewing methods to assess their impact on air-gap flux density and torque pulsations. The findings demonstrate AM’s potential to advance electric machine efficiency, supporting sustainable development in the automotive industry.

papers.title: Modern approach to the prevention of venous thromboembolic complications in patients before and after hip arthroplasty
papers.abstract: Background. The problem of diagnosis and prevention of postoperative coagulopathies is quite relevant in modern orthopaedics, since an increasing number of patients with various pathologies of the hip joints undergo arthroplasty both in Ukraine and abroad. The purpose: based on the analysis of risk factors for the development of venous thromboembolic complications in patients with hip joint pathology after arthroplasty, to substantiate a set of measures for their prevention. Materials and methods. Patients who underwent hip arthroplasty were divided into the following groups: group I — low risk, 20–40 years old (n = 13); group II — moderate risk, 41–60 years old (n = 45); group III — high risk, 61–80 years old (n = 42). To assess the risk of thrombotic complications, a method similar to the J.A. Caprini score was used. Results. Analysis of thrombotic complications in the studied groups of patients after total hip replacement compared to the data of the scientific literature showed that complications in the form of pulmonary embolism were not observed in our patients. According to the literature, they are found in 1.08–30 % of cases. Deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremities was detected in 4.65 and 10–20 % of patients, respectively (an average decrease of 5.35 %), oedema of the lower extremities (chronic venous insufficiency) — in 15.5–20.9 and 17–25 % of cases (an average decrease of 3 %). Conclusions. Thromboprophylaxis of venous thromboembolic complications during total hip arthroplasty requires an individual approach to patients, taking into account risk factors both in the pre-operative and postoperative periods. The prevention program we proposed in the studied patients, compared to the literature data, allowed us to reduce the number of thrombotic complications: in group I of patients with a low risk, these complications were not observed, in groups II and III, deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremities decreased by 5.35 %, oedema of the lower extremities by 3 %, hematomas in the surgical area by 1.5 %. The data obtained indicate the effectiveness and feasibility of using a set of thromboprophylaxis measures proposed by us in patients after hip arthroplasty.

papers.title: Prediction of Mechanical Property of Metal 3D Printed Parts Affected by Process Interruptions Using Machine Learning Method
papers.abstract: Abstract Metal additive manufacturing (AM) enables rapid prototyping and decentralized production, enhancing supply chain resilience. However, process interruptions during fabrication can disrupt melting-solidification cycles, leading to microstructural inconsistencies that degrade mechanical properties. This study investigates the impact of such interruptions on stainless steel 316L parts fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM), both with and without postprocessing. A network-based approach is introduced to model mechanical property variations using graph structures, where nodes represent grains or pores and edges capture stress-transfer pathways. Graph metrics—such as degree centrality, betweenness, and clustering coefficient identify regions prone to mechanical failure. Fabricated samples are analyzed using nano-indentation to assess hardness and elasticity, complemented by ultrasonic NDT, optical microscopy, and SEM. To assess recovery, a subset of samples undergoes vacuum heat treatment. Post-treatment properties are compared to evaluate improvement in material homogeneity. Machine learning techniques, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), predict mechanical performance based on microstructural patterns. Findings show that interruptions reduce uniformity in mechanical properties, while post-processing mitigates these effects. Network-based analysis, combined with predictive modeling, offers a powerful tool for optimizing process parameters and improving the reliability of metal AM components.
